title: Checkpoint 12: Stockfish (skill 0) vs Magnus
notes: Checkpoint after game 12, from the Queen's Gambit Declined: Magnus plays the yardstick, Stockfish at skill 0. Nothing is studied afterwards.

moves.thought: I must block the check on the a4–e8 diagonal while developing; 5...Nbd7 interposes a defended piece (Qd8 covers d7, and no pawn or piece wins it) and keeps the normal QGD structure, whereas 5...c6 blocks my c-pawn and 5...Bd7/Qd7 are passive or walk into Bxf6 ideas. I checked White's tries: 6.cxd5 exd5 is fine, and 6.Nb5 Nc7+ never works since my queen guards c7.

This is the standard Queen's Gambit Declined with 5.Qa4+ Nbd7 6.e3; my development is nearly complete and the king should get out of the centre before I commit to ...c6 or ...dxc4. I checked that after 0-0 nothing hangs: the Nd7 is attacked once along the a4-e8 diagonal but still defended by the queen, and White has no capture or check that wins material.

My king is castled and the central break ...c5 hits White's d4/c4 duo immediately; after 8.dxc5 Nxc5 or 8.cxd5 exd5 9.dxc5 Nxc5 everything is defended and the Qa4 has no tactic on a7/d7. I avoided ...h6 (pawn move in front of my king with Bg5 aimed there) and the passive ...c6, since nothing of mine can be taken by a pawn after ...c5.

Taking with 8...cxd4 forces 9.exd4 (9.Nxd4 allows ...dxc4 comfortably), after which 9...dxc4 10.Bxc4 Nb6 leaves White with an isolated d-pawn and me with easy play and no loose pieces. I rejected 8...Ne4 because after 9.Bxe7 Qxe7 10.Nxe4 dxe4 11.Qxe4 the unsupported knight simply costs a pawn — exactly the "advanced piece with no pawn support" error from my notebook.

Taking on c4 is the standard freeing move here: after 10.Bxc4 White is left with an isolated d-pawn while my structure is sound, and I gain the tempo ...Nb6 hitting the bishop. I rejected 9...Ne4 because it is unsupported and drops a pawn to 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxe4 dxe4 12.Qxe4, exactly the "advanced knight with no pawn support" error from my notebook.

I must recapture on f6, and gxf6 would wreck my castled king's pawn shield, while Nxf6 leaves my e7 bishop passive and blocks the knight; Bxf6 recaptures with the minor piece, puts immediate pressure on White's isolated d4 pawn, and keeps the Nd7 flexible (Nb6 to support my extra c4 pawn). I checked White's replies: 11.Bxc4 Nb6 is comfortable, and 11.d5 exd5 12.Nxd5 Be5/Bxb2 is fine for me, with nothing of mine left loose.

Bxd4 is a trap since Nf3 guards d4 (bishop for a pawn), so I looked for a developing move with tempo: Nb6 hits the c4 bishop, and after Bb3/Bd3 I follow with Bd7/Rc8; I checked 12.d5 exd5 13.Nxd5 Nxd5 14.Bxd5 and the resulting trades are fine for me, while b6 can never be hit by a pawn.

The d4 pawn is attacked twice (Bf6 and Qd8 down the open d-file) and defended only once (Nf3), so 12...Bxd4 13.Nxd4 Qxd4 just wins a clean central pawn; crucially Nb5 is unavailable to harass my queen because White's own bishop sits on b5, and Nd5 tricks fail to exd5/Nxd5. After 14.Rd1 Qf6 I follow with a6, Bd7 and consolidate a healthy extra pawn.

My Bd4 is attacked by Nf3 but defended by Qd8, so instead of retreating I grab a tempo with 13...a6 hitting the b5 bishop; a6 is covered twice (b7 and Ra8), so Bxa6 just loses a piece, and tricks like 14.Na4 axb5 15.Nxb6 Qxb6 or 14.Ne4 axb5 15.Nd6 Qxd6 win material for me. If White saves the bishop with 14.Be2 or trades 14.Nxd4 Qxd4 (when the bishop is still hanging to ...axb5), I keep my extra pawn and then consolidate with Bf6/Bd7.

White's knight on d4 is completely undefended — Nc3 covers d5/e4/b5 but not d4, Qc2 has no line to d4, and neither rook touches it, so 14...Qxd4 immediately recovers the piece and leaves me a clean pawn up with the extra point that Bb5 is still attacked by my a6 pawn. I checked White's tries: 15.Rad1/Rfd1 only chase the queen (Rd1 is defended, so no Qxd1 needed) while the bishop hangs, and 15.Bc4 runs into Nxc4; there are no checks or forks against my king.

White's Bd3/Qc2 battery threatens Bxh7+ (Kxh7 is illegal because the queen recaptures through the opened diagonal), so I must defuse it to keep my extra pawn; I also rejected the tempting queen moves Qxf2+, Qxc3, Qc4, Qd5, Qe4, Qa4 and Qe3 because each loses the queen to Rxf2, bxc3, Bxc4, Nxd5/Nxe4/Nxa4 or fxe3. 15...h6 steps the pawn off the light-squared battery's target (my remaining bishop-free dark squares are covered by g7 and Rf8), after which I consolidate with Bd7/Rfd8 a clean pawn up.

My Qd4 effectively pins the c3-knight to b2 (any knight move allows ...Qxb2 and after the queen trade I'd be two pawns up), so instead of moving the queen I should fix my real problem — the undeveloped bishop and rook. Bd7 is attacked by nothing (Rd1's file is blocked by Bd3, and no pawn or piece covers d7), it defends a6 and e6, and tactics like Bb5, Nb5, Na4 or Bxa6 all fail to ...Qxb2 or simple recaptures.
Only one legal move exists — the bishop check on h7 forces my king to h8, after which White's bishop must retreat and I keep my extra pawn.

White's whole bind is Qc2+Bh7 freezing my king, so 18...f5 blocks the b1-h7 diagonal and leaves the bishop undefended — 19.Rd6? or any slow move runs into ...Kxh7, and 19.Bxf5 exf5 fails to 20.Qxf5?? Rxf5 since my f-file is open, so I even regain a piece. White's best is 19.Bg6, when ...Rf6 and ...Kg8 harass the bishop and free my king; pushing f5 breaks rule 13's spirit but here it is a forcing tempo move that removes the attacking diagonal rather than opening one.

My bishop on d7 is hanging to the doubled rooks, while White's bishop on h7 is trapped behind my f5 pawn (g8 is covered by Rf8), so 19...Kxh7 20.Rxd7 would just trade one bishop for the other and leave me a clean queen down. Instead 19...Be8 saves my bishop and simultaneously guards g6, the only flight square, so Bh7 is lost next move with ...Kxh7; I checked e8 is hit by no pawn, rook or queen, and Qxf5 fails to exf5.

White's bishop on h7 is trapped and completely undefended — the queen's c2-h7 diagonal is blocked by my own f5 pawn, and no rook covers h7 — so Kxh7 simply wins a whole piece. The only consequence is 21.Qxf5+ regaining a pawn with check, after which 21...Kh8 keeps me solid; delaying with f4 or Bf7 risks 21.Bg6 or 21.Rxe6 ideas, so I take the free piece at once.

My knight on b6 is hanging to Re6, so I must move it: Nd5 drops to Nxd5/Rxd5, Na4 to Nxa4, and Nd7 fails to 22.Rxe8 Rxe8 23.Rxd7 since the bishop that defended d7 would be gone. Nc4 is the only square no pawn, piece or queen currently covers (Qc2 is blocked by its own Nc3), it eyes b2 and d6, and if White kicks with b3 I retreat to the strong d6 square guarding e8 and f5.

White's main threat is 23.Qxf5+ snatching my loose pawn with check, and secondarily any knight move opening the c-file for Qxc4, so I need to cover f5 without putting a piece where a pawn or rook wins it (Ne3 falls to fxe3, Na3 to bxa3, Nb6/Nd6/Ne5 to the rook on e6, Nxb2 to Qxb2). 22...Bg6 defends f5, is protected by my king (so Rxg6 Kxg6 would just lose a rook for a bishop), activates my worst piece, and leaves Rf8 guarding the e8 square; if White then plays Ne2 or Nd5 to open the c-file I answer with ...b5, propping up the knight on c4.

The b3 pawn hits my knight, and I checked every knight square: Nb2/Nd2 drop to Qxd2/Qxb2, Na3 loses to Qb2, Ne3 to Rxe3 or fxe3, Nd6/Ne5 to Rxd6/Rxe5, and Nb6 invites Na4 trading my knight off when I can't afford simplification. Na5 is attacked by nothing, pokes at b3, and keeps the route Na5-c6 where the knight would cover a7, b8 and e7 against White's rook invasion on the seventh.

My knight on a5 is loose and offside — White threatens Re5 forking a5 and f5 — so I bring it back to c6 where the b7 pawn supports it (Rxc6 bxc6 would just lose a rook for a knight) and it covers d4, e5, e7 and b4. I checked that after Nc6 every other unit is defended: a6 by Ra8, f5 by Rf8, and the attacked Bg6 by my king, while Nd4 ideas hitting e6 and b3 give me some counterplay.

I checked that White's only real break is Nc3-d5 heading for Nf6+/Ne7, so I bring my dead a8-rook to the open file where it both covers d5 (making Nd5 simply lose a piece to Rxd5) and activates my worst piece; I rejected 25...Nd4 (26.Rd6 kicks the loose knight), 25...Ne5 (Rxe5 outright), 25...Rae8 (Rxe8 Rxe8 Rxe8 Bxe8 trades into a hopeless queen-vs-two-minors ending) and noted ...Rd2 ideas are impossible since Qb2 covers d2.

My bishop on g6 is attacked by both the h5 pawn and Re6, so I must resolve it; Bxh5 grabs the pawn since no white piece covers h5 (Re1 is blocked by my own h6 pawn, and the e-rook can't reach it). Alternatives like Rf6 or Nd4 all allow hxg6+ winning my bishop for a pawn, so taking is clearly best.

I checked that d4 is untouchable — Qb2's diagonal is blocked by its own knight on c3, the a3/b3 pawns don't cover d4, and Nc3 doesn't reach it — so 27...Nd4 centralises with tempo against the deep Re6 (and if Re4 tries to attack it, Rxd4 Rxd4 just loses rook for knight since Rd8 defends). I rejected 27...Rd6 and 27...Rf6 after playing the chain out: Rxd6 has no recapture, and Rf6 invites an even rook trade, which only helps White's queen in a three-pieces-versus-queen fight.

I'm down queen for bishop-and-pawn, so I need a solid move that stops White's Re7 invasion against my loose b7/g7 pawns rather than a tactic — Nf3+ fails to gxf3, Ne2+/Nc2 just drop material to Nxe2/Qxc2, and f4 loses the pawn after Re5/Nd5 while loosening my king. 28...Rd7 covers the whole seventh rank, blocks e7, is attacked by nothing, and keeps my centralized knight and bishop coordinated for defence.

White's 29.Qb1 opened the b1-h7 diagonal and threatens Qxf5+ winning a pawn with check, and my tactical tries all fail (Nc2 drops to Qxc2, Ne2+/Nf3+ to Rxe2/gxf3, Nxb3 to Qxb3, Rd5 to Nxd5). So I defend f5 with my bishop, which lands on g6 protected by my king and keeps my pawn structure intact rather than committing to ...g6 where f3-g4 could harass the bishop.

White's Qb2 renews the threat of 31.Ne2, hitting my d4-knight twice (knight plus the b2-queen once c3 clears) while it is only defended by Rd7, so I must address it. Retreating 30...Nc6 keeps the knight safe (attacked by nothing, extra-guarded by b7), covers the key e7 invasion square so Re7 is impossible, and avoids any trade of pieces, which I can't afford being down queen for bishop and pawn.

I'm material down (queen for bishop), so my priority is removing loose pieces and threats: the d7 rook, b7 pawn and g6 bishop are all hanging to ideas like Re7, Re6 and g4. Rff7 connects my rooks on the seventh so they defend each other, b7, g7 and (with the bishop) the f5 pawn, and if White trades both rooks on e7 I reach queen versus bishop+knight with an extra pawn, which is my best practical defence.

I rechecked defenders on f3 and saw the g2 pawn guards it, so Ne5 (fxe5) and Rd3 (only an even trade) are pointless, while Rd4 drops material to Ne2. Nd4 centralises with tempo: it threatens Nxf3+ gxf3 winning rook for knight, it blocks the b2–g7 diagonal, and it stays defended by Rd7 (with Rf7 backing d7), so 33.Ne2 fails to Nxf3+ and 33.Rxd4 Rxd4 would just lose a rook for a knight.

I'm down queen-for-bishop, so I must avoid rook trades and keep every unit defended; Ne2+/Nf3+/Ne6/Nxb3/Nc2/Rd5 all drop a piece to Nxe2, gxf3, Rxe6, Qxb3, Qxc2 and Nxd5 respectively. 33...Rd6 keeps all pieces: it defends my strong Nd4, guards g6 a second time so Rxg6 only loses a rook for the bishop, covers a6 and h6, controls d5 against Nd5, and leaves Rf7 holding f5 and g7.

White's 34.Na2 opened the b2–d4 diagonal, but my knight on d4 is held by Rd6, and nothing of mine is hanging; immediate 34...Ne2+/Nf3+ just drop the knight to Rxe2 or gxf3 (rule 1). Instead 34...Bh5 keeps everything defended and creates a real threat of 35...Ne2+, since then 36.Rxe2 Bxe2 wins rook for knight and anything else lets ...Nxg3 win a rook outright; if White tries 35.g4 then 35...fxg4 leaves my bishop supported by the new g4 pawn while White's king gets airy.

I checked the tempting fork 35...Ne2+ but counted the capture chain to the end: 36.Rxe2 Bxe2 37.Qxe2 (the queen also eyes e2 along the second rank), so I'd give knight and bishop for a rook — exactly the error my rule 3 warns about. Instead White's real threat is Rg3-d3, piling on Nd4 with Qb2 against a single defender, so I double rooks on the d-file; the knight stays as a blockader on d4 also blocking the b2-h8 diagonal (Qf6/Qe5 are impossible, and after Rd3 the whole exchange on d4 wins material for me), while Rg5 hitting f5/h5 is simply met by ...Bg6.

Down queen for bishop, I need active counterplay, and 36...Ne2 forks the f4 pawn and the Rg3 while being defended by my Bh5, with no white pawn able to hit e2 (g2 only covers f3/h3). If White takes with 37.Rxe2 Bxe2 I win a rook for the knight, and 37.Rge3/37.Rg5 both allow 37...Nxf4 picking up a pawn with my knight hopping into d3 to hit the queen next.

My knight on e2 is hit twice by the rooks and undefended, so it must move, and f4 is the one escape square that grabs a pawn while being attacked by nothing (no pawn, queen, rook or knight covers f4) and it also guards my loose bishop on h5. I checked the kicks: 38.Rf3 or 38.Qf2 run into 38...Nd3! forking b2/f2 and e1, and after 38.Re7 Rxe7 39.Rxe7 the mate idea Qf6/Qxg7# is stopped by 39...Nd5 hitting the rook and covering f6.

White's 38.Qc2 threatens Qxf5+ followed by Qxf4 (and even Qxh5), so I must stop that diagonal; instead of passively defending with Bg6 or Rd5, 38...Nd3 blocks the c2-f5 diagonal, lands on a square covered by both my rooks (and untouchable since Qxd3 Rxd3 wins the queen, with b3/a4 pawns unable to reach d3), and simultaneously hits Re1 and f2 — so 39.Rf3? Nxe1 wins a rook outright and White must spend a tempo moving the e1 rook.

White's Rxd3 took my knight, which was defended twice on the d-file, so I simply must recapture — after 39...Rxd3 my rook on d3 is defended by Rd7, so Qxd3?? Rxd3 would lose the queen for a rook, and any other move just gifts White a free knight. I checked White's replies: 40.Re7 Rxe7 wins a rook for me, and there are no checks or forks available to White.

My Rd3 is hit twice (Qc2 and the new Nb4) and defended once, so I must move it, and d4 is a square no White piece or pawn touches while it keeps both rooks linked (Rd4 defends Rd7 and vice versa) and attacks the undefended Nb4 plus a4. I checked every knight escape — Nd5 Rxd5, Nc6 bxc6, Nxa6 bxa6, Na2 Rd2!, Nd3 Rxd3 Qxd3 Rxd3 — so the piece falls; the only real counter 41.Qxf5+ is met by 41...Bg6 blocking and hitting the queen (42.Qxg6+ Kxg6 wins the queen), after which 42...Rxb4 nets the knight.

White's immediate threat is Qxf5+, so I must defend f5 while keeping my rooks mutually protecting each other on the d-file (Rxb4 fails to Qxb4, Rc4/Rc7 drop a rook to the queen, Rh4+ and Rf4 leave Rd7 loose for Re7). Bg6 guards f5, the bishop is safe behind my king, and my doubled rooks stay so strong that 42.Rd1 Rxd1+ or 42.Re4 Rxe4 just win a rook outright; I prefer Bg6 to g6 so I don't loosen the pawns around my king.

White's 42.a5 fixed my a6 pawn and threatened Nxa6, so I need a defender; 42...R7d6 guards a6 along the sixth rank (Nxa6 Rxa6 wins the knight) while Rd4 keeps the knight pinned to its only defender, Qc5. I checked the capture chains: Qxd6 Rxd4... actually Rxd6 wins queen for rook, and tries like 43.Nc6 or 43.Nc2 are met by Rd5, hitting the queen while staying defended by Rd6.

My Rd4 is hit twice (Qc5 and Nc2) and only defended once, but I noticed the knight on c2 is completely undefended, so Rd2 saves the rook, invades the second rank, and attacks the loose knight while still guarding Rd6 along the d-file. I verified no White pawn (a5, b3, g2) can touch d2, that Qxd6 Rxd6 just loses the queen for a rook, and that once Re1 leaves the first rank my ...Rd1+ back-rank resource appears.

R6d5 attacks the queen while staying defended by Rd2 (Qxd5 Rxd5 wins the queen for a rook), and because my rook stays on d2 hitting the knight, White's queen can only step along the c-file — any queen move off c2's defence loses the knight to Rxc2. I rejected Rxc2 (Qxc2 defends it) and Rxg2 (Kxg2), and R2d5 is worse because it abandons the pressure on c2.

I first checked Rxa5 and Rxc2 — both lose a rook, since Qc3 guards a5 via b4 and defends the c2 knight — and I rejected Re5/R5d4 (Qxe5, Nxd4) plus the rook trade with Rd1, which would strip me down to R+B against Q+N. R5d3 keeps a rook on the second rank, is protected by Rd2, and hits the queen (Qxd3 Rxd3 wins Q for R) while also hitting b3; if the queen steps off the b2/c2 guard, Rxc2 picks up the knight.

b3 is completely undefended (Nc2 covers a1/a3/b4/d4/e1/e3, Qc5 covers only the c-file and b4/b5/b6), so Rxb3 wins a clean pawn while Rd2 still pins the queen to the defence of c2 — if the queen ever leaves the c-file, ...Rxc2 wins the knight. I checked White's tries: Qxf5 is met by Bxf5 (so I keep the bishop on g6 guarding f5), Qd4 runs into Rxc2, and Nd4/Nb4 allow ...Rb2 with the deadly ...Rxg2 mate threat since the rook on b2 would stop Kxg2.

My b3-rook is attacked by Nd4, and I must retreat it — but rule 1 saved me from 47...Rh3+/Rf3, since the g2 pawn simply takes (gxh3/gxf3), and Rb4/Rb6/Ra3/Rc3 all drop to Qc5 while Rb5 falls to Nxb5 and Rxd4 just loses a rook to Qxd4. Rbb2 puts the rook on a square untouched by queen, knight, rook or pawn, has the two rooks defending each other on the second rank, keeps Rd2 hitting g2 (threatening Rxg2 with Rb2 recapturing, after which Rh2+ and Rbg2 mate ideas loom), and even rules out 48.Rd1 since Rxd1+ would be check with nothing to recapture.

My pawn on f5 was already attacked by Nd4 and could be hit a second time (Qd5 then Nxf5), so I push it: 48...f4 is captured by nothing, opens the b1-h7 diagonal for my bishop (so Qf5+ or Qe4+ simply lose the queen to Bxf5/Bxe4, and White now has no checks at all), and starts the real plan of ...f3 plus my rooks on the second rank, where after gxf3 a rook landing on h3 is mate since Rb2 denies g2 to his king. I checked knight tries: Ne6 or Qe5 hitting f4 is met by ...Rf2 defending, and Ne2 loses to Rxe2.

My d2 rook is attacked by Nf3, and I must move it — but Rd1/Rb1 lose to Rxd1 on the open first rank, and Rd4/Rd5/Rd6/Rb4/Rb5/Rb6 all drop the rook to Qc5, while Rxg2 liquidates into a lost queen-versus-rook ending. Rf2 keeps the rooks connected (Rb2 guards f2, so Qxf2 Rxf2 wins the queen), attacks the blockading knight on f3, defends my key f4 pawn against Qf5/Qd4, and prepares ...f3 the moment the knight steps away.

I spotted the trap in the natural 50...Rbd2 attacking the queen: 51.Qxd2 Rxd2 52.Nxd2! (the f3 knight covers d2) leaves me with only bishop and pawns against rook and knight, so I played the capture chain out and rejected it. Ra2 keeps my rooks mutually defended along the second rank (so Qxf2/Qxa2 always loses the queen for a rook), keeps f4 and g7 guarded, and attacks the loose a5 pawn; I checked White's checks (Ng5+ hxg5 just drops a knight, Qe4+/Qd3+ are blocked by my bishop on g6) and found no knight fork hitting a2/f2.

The a5 pawn is completely undefended (Qf4, Nf3 and Rg1 none cover it), so Rxa5 wins a clean pawn and, more importantly, kills White's only potential passer while leaving my a6/b7 pair as the healthy majority; after the natural tempo hits 52.Qd4/Qc3 (hitting f2 and g7) I simply return with ...Ra2, re-doubling on the second rank where White's king, rook and knight stay passive. I checked Rxg2 (Rxg2 Rxg2 Rxg2 Kxg2 loses two rooks for rook and pawn) and Rxf3 (gxf3 leaves me with rook and bishop versus queen and rook) — both lose material, and after Rxa5 no queen check or knight fork hits both rooks.

White's Qd4 hits my loose rook on f2 along the d4-e3-f2 diagonal, so I must address it, but Rxf3 (gxf3) and Rxg2/Rf1 all just drop material to the g2 pawn or Rg1. Raa2 defends f2 along the clear second rank (so Qxf2 Rxf2 wins the queen, and nothing recaptures on f2), doubles my rooks against White's boxed-in king, keeps a6 covered on the a-file, and avoids any rook trade — trades favour White's Q+N here.

My bishop on g6 is attacked by Qg4 and only "defended" by Kh7, and 54.Ne5 followed by Nxg6 wins it outright since Kxg6 would be illegal on the open g-file — so Kg8/Kh8 drop the piece, and h5 loses it too after Ng5+ (the h6 pawn is what currently denies g5). I checked Be4/Bf5/Bh5 all fall to the queen, so I retreat to c2, where both rooks defend the bishop, it blocks the b1-h7 diagonal against Qe4+/Qf5+, and my h6/g7 shelter stays intact.

g2 is only defended by the king and the queen along the g-file, so 54...Rxg2 55.Qxg2 Rxg2 56.Kxg2 trades both rooks for the queen and pawn, killing White's Ng5+/Qh-file attacking ideas and leaving me bishop plus four pawns against a lone knight — a trivially winning endgame. I checked the alternatives: Rf1+ and Rxf3 just drop material, and if White declines with 55.Re7 I simply take the queen with Rxg4.

I checked the capture chain to the end: 55...hxg5 wins a knight, and 56.Qxg5?? simply loses the queen to 56...Rxg5 since my g2-rook hits g5 along the open g-file and nothing defends the queen. White's only tries are spite checks (56.Qe4+ Rg6! blocks with the rook defended by my king, 56.Qxg2 Bxg2+ 57.Kxg2 leaves me rook and four pawns against a bare rook), so taking the piece is clearly best over any king retreat.

I'm forced to move my king, and I see that my Rg2 is hanging to Qxg2 (my Ra2 doesn't defend it because my own bishop on c2 blocks the second rank), so the rook falls either way. Therefore I choose the king square that keeps me safest from follow-up checks and mating nets: on g8 my g7 pawn shields the g-file and Re8+/Qc8+ only give me repetition-type checks, whereas on g6 my king is in the open where the queen and rook could hunt it down and pick off my pawns.

I'm up two rooks and a bishop for the queen, so my only job is to pick the escape square that gives White the fewest safe checks: from h7 my g7 pawn blocks all rank-7 checks and my Bc2 covers d3/e4/f5/g6, so Qd3+/Qe4+/Qf5+/Qg6+ all simply lose the queen to Bxd3/Bxe4/Bxf5/Kxg6, leaving only Qh3+. By contrast Kh8 allows Qe8+/Re8+/Qh6+/Qh3+ with real mating nets on the back rank, and Kf8 walks into a swarm of checks (Qc8+, Qd6+, Re8+).

Kg8 would repeat the position after 56...Kg8 and let White claim a threefold repetition draw with Qe6+/Qh3+, which I must avoid while up two rooks and a bishop for the queen. Kg6 steps out of the repetition and is safe: Qh5+ would simply be met by Kxh5, and the natural 59.Qd3+ loses the queen to Bxd3 since my bishop already covers d3, leaving White only Qe6+ (when Kh6 is a new square) or the unprotected Re6+, which I answer with Kf7/Kxe7 ideas.

My bishop on c2 is hit by Qg2 (though defended by Ra2), and White threatens Re6+ picking up pawns, so I want a move that is safe from any capture and shores up both. Bf5 is defended by my king, blocks the e4/d5 checking diagonals, guards e6 so Re6+ loses the rook to Bxe6, and simultaneously covers c2/d3 so that any queen raid along the second rank (Qd2/Qb2) is met by Rc2 hitting the queen with the bishop's support; b5 is exactly the unescorted pawn push my notebook warns about.

My bishop on f5 is perfect where it is — it covers d3, e4, g4 and h3, taking away almost every queen check, and moves like Bd3/Bg4/Bh3 just drop it to the queen while Be4+ loses to Rxe4. White's real threat was Qb8/Qc7 hitting the loose b7 pawn (g7 is already guarded by my king), so I advance it to b5 where the a6 pawn defends it and I get connected passers to run with the rook behind them.

Every king move (Kf7/Kh5/Kh6/Kh7) loses the bishop to Qxf5 since the king only guards f5 from g6, and Rg2/Rh2+/Re2 simply drop the rook to Kxg2/Kxh2/Rxe2, so the rook must stay active elsewhere. Qe5 is hitting b5, and Rb2 defends it from behind while keeping my rook on the second rank and ready to escort the b-pawn (b4-b3 would be covered by the rook) — unlike the passive Ra5, which ties my rook down and blocks my own queenside counterplay.

I'm down to bishop and four pawns against queen and rook, so my only job is to avoid losing material immediately — Be4+ runs into Rxe4, and every pawn move (a5, b4, g4) drops a pawn to the queen since a6 must stay to guard b5. Moving the bishop to the quiet c8 square keeps it off the e- and d-files and off any check/skewer line, while my king still shields g5 and g7.

Blocking with Bf5 just loses the bishop to Qxf5+, so I must step the king; Kf6 keeps the king central, still guards g5, and avoids the edge lines after Kh5/Kh6 where Qg4+/Qc1 ideas hit my pawns. If White tries Re6+ my bishop simply takes the undefended rook.

Be6 loses the bishop outright because the rook on e1 guards e6, so Qxe6+ just wins a piece; Kf5 walks into Re5+/Qd5+ with my king in the open. Kf7 keeps the bishop and gives my king shelter near g7 with no immediate mate.
Only one legal move exists — Kf6 is forced after Qe8+.
Only one legal move is available, so there is nothing to calculate — Kg6 is forced.

Be6 just loses the bishop to Qxe6+, and Kh5 walks into Qd1+ or Re5 ideas with my king trapped on the edge; Kf7 keeps the bishop and gives the king escape squares on both f8/g8 and g6. I'm already lost on material, so my only plan is to hold the bishop and g7 pawn and avoid forced mate.
